You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test `testEqualsCS1()` calls `StringUtils.equals` with two `StringBuilder` instances. The method `StringUtils.equals` implementation first checks for reference equality and nulls, then if both arguments are `String` types, it uses `String.equals()`. Otherwise, it calls `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches` with the two sequences and passes `length` as the maximum of the two sequences' lengths.

The critical problem lies in line 81 of `StringUtils.equals`:
```
return CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches(cs1, false, 0, cs2, 0, Math.max(cs1.length(), cs2.length()));
```
This call uses `Math.max(cs1.length(), cs2.length())` as the length of the region to match. If `cs1` and `cs2` have differing lengths, this leads to `regionMatches` attempting to access characters beyond the end of the shorter sequence, causing a `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

Within `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches`, the loop iterates for `length` times, accessing `cs.charAt(index1++)` and `substring.charAt(index2++)`. Since the `length` parameter can be larger than the shorter sequence's length, this access is out-of-bound.

The correct approach is to use the minimum length of the two sequences when comparing character regions to avoid out-of-bounds access. This mistake explains why the test with differently sized `StringBuilder`s (`"abc"` vs `"abcd"`) fails with a `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` rather than returning false safely.

No relevant recent bug reports directly relate to this bug. Therefore, the bug is due to this misuse of length in `StringUtils.equals`.

Summary: The bug occurs because `StringUtils.equals` passes the maximum length of the two sequences to `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches` instead of the minimum length, leading to an index-out-of-bounds exception when the sequences differ in length.

Next, it is advisable to fix `StringUtils.equals(CharSequence, CharSequence)` method to use minimum length when calling `regionMatches`.
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The `testEqualsCS1()` test fails due to a `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException` caused by the `StringUtils.equals(CharSequence cs1, CharSequence cs2)` method. The method compares two `CharSequence` objects but incorrectly uses the maximum length of the two sequences when calling `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches`. Inside `regionMatches`, this length is used to loop over characters of both sequences, resulting in out-of-bounds access when one sequence is shorter than the other.

Specifically, line 81 in `StringUtils.equals` calls:
```java
CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches(cs1, false, 0, cs2, 0, Math.max(cs1.length(), cs2.length()))
```
whereas it should use the minimum length of the two sequences to safely compare characters without exceeding either sequence’s length.

The `CharSequenceUtils.regionMatches` method relies on the length parameter to iterate through characters, expecting it to be within the bounds of both sequences. Passing the maximum length causes the iteration to overrun the shorter sequence, leading to the index-out-of-bounds exception observed.

This explains why the test fails when comparing `new StringBuilder("abc")` with `new StringBuilder("abcd")`.

No recent bug reports provide additional insights; the issue is straightforwardly a logic error in length calculation when comparing sequences.

The fix involves changing the length argument in the call to `regionMatches` from `Math.max(...)` to `Math.min(...)`.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
